nuggets.summary: Oki describes the pivotal Windows-vs-OS/2 decision at Microsoft: rather than hedging by continuing to develop applications for both platforms, he pushed the board to give OS/2 back to IBM entirely and focus applications development solely on Windows. Every major software competitor (Lotus, Ashton-Tate, Borland, Software Publishers) was betting the other way, porting their character-based applications to OS/2 instead. When OS/2 failed in the market, Microsoft was the only company with a mature Windows application suite and instantly dominated a category it had previously been "nowhere" in. The generalizable point he draws is that a full, uncomfortable commitment to one horse -- even when it isn't obviously the optimal call at the time -- can beat a hedged position, because a hedge means you're never fully positioned to capture the win if your bet is right.

When Oki built Microsoft's international division from scratch, he set one non-negotiable hiring filter for every person he brought on: they had to have prior startup experience, regardless of whether that startup succeeded or failed. He treated having gone through the startup grind at all -- win or lose -- as the relevant signal, not a track record of wins. This is a specific, reusable screening heuristic for anyone building a scrappy, high-ambiguity team: prior exposure to startup conditions predicts fit better than prior success does.

Despite being heavily sought after as a mentor given his track record, Oki says he actively avoids one-on-one mentoring and does very little of it. His stated reasoning is that mentoring is inherently a one-to-one activity, and because time is the one resource he can never create more of (unlike money), he'd rather spend it on activities that let him influence many people at once rather than a single mentee. This runs against the usual expectation that a successful, generous person with a mission statement about "encouraging others" should be a heavy mentor -- his actual behavior is to deliberately opt out of the highest-touch, lowest-leverage version of that impulse.

Asked what separates nonprofits likely to survive from those that won't, Oki names a specific milestone: whether the organization has a predictable revenue stream, as opposed to relying on one-off gifts, an annual gala, or ad hoc donor asks. Once revenue becomes predictable -- from any source, donor-based or earned -- he says the organization's risk profile drops sharply, and he actively pushes the nonprofit leaders he works with to identify and build toward that predictability rather than treating fundraising as a series of independent asks. This is a direct nonprofit analog to the startup emphasis on recurring revenue over one-time deals.

Oki gives a concrete financial-health benchmark he checks on every nonprofit balance sheet he reviews: at least a full year of operating costs held in the bank, so that if the donor base or an annual gala dries up, the organization has a year of runway to recover rather than collapsing immediately. He notes this is rare in practice -- most nonprofits are living day to day with no such buffer -- which makes it a useful diagnostic for donors or board members trying to assess whether an organization is actually stable versus one crisis away from failure.
nuggets.wedge_note: Nonprofit financial-health/runway scoring from public 990 filings, for donors and grantmakers doing due diligence on which orgs are stable; validate by interviewing foundation program officers.

nuggets.summary: Recounting a performance review early in his Microsoft career, Oki told Bill Gates he'd worked three straight years without taking a single day off, expecting some acknowledgment. Gates's blunt reply -- "so what, I've worked seven years without a day off" -- reveals that in that environment, extreme hours weren't a heroic outlier being rewarded; they were the unremarkable baseline the founder himself was already exceeding. The transferable point for anyone leading through personal example: if you're asking a team for extraordinary effort, the credible version of that ask is the leader quietly already doing more, not announcing the sacrifice and expecting special credit for it.

Oki required everyone reporting to him, and himself even more so, to work roughly 100-hour weeks ("if they're going to work 100 hour weeks, I had to work 101"). When marriage and children made that pace unsustainable, he discovered there was no way to gradually dial it back once that reputation was established -- "you create a reputation of working 100 hours a week... at some point in time, you can't do it." His actual exit wasn't a negotiated reduction in hours; it was a full resignation, timed to land exactly ten years to the day from his start date. The lesson for anyone who has built a leadership identity on extreme output: expect the exit to be a clean break, not a graceful throttle-down, because the reputation itself makes a partial retreat look like a broken promise.

Asked whether Microsoft's OS/2-versus-Windows maneuvering contributed to its later antitrust case, Oki volunteers an unexpected personal position: he actually wishes the Justice Department had broken up Microsoft, because as an entrepreneur he personally dislikes "big monster companies" and prefers smaller ones. Coming from someone whose entire fortune was built inside that company, this is a notable break from the expected loyalty narrative, and a reminder that people who profited enormously from consolidation don't necessarily believe consolidation is good.

Oki's grassroots Parents Union aimed to sign up a million Washington parents for free, no-cost membership as a counterweight to the teachers union in Olympia; it landed only about 10,000. He contrasts this with the teachers union's 83,000 dues-paying members (whose dues are compulsory payroll deductions, funding paid lobbyists), and notes that engagement was hardest to get precisely from the parents who'd benefit most -- inner-city families without the bandwidth to organize. The transferable insight for anyone building a counter-movement or advocacy campaign: a free, opt-in membership drive structurally underperforms an organized interest group with compulsory dues and paid staff, and the people with the most at stake are often the least able to participate in a voluntary campaign.

Oki argues that most nonprofits get their CEO's job description backward: the common setup is that the CEO does no fundraising at all, delegating that entirely to a development officer, while Oki believes raising capital should be a core part of the top job -- treating the organization like a business that must build durable access to capital rather than "going back to the well" of the same donors every single year. This reframes the CEO's primary output in a nonprofit as capital access, not just program execution, which is a different hiring and evaluation bar than most boards apply.

As part of his public-education reform pitch, Oki points out a specific structural mismatch: a typical corporate CEO controls 100% of their company's budget, while a public school principal -- functionally the "CEO" of their school -- controls only about 5% of the school's budget, because hiring, firing, and most administrative decisions are made elsewhere in the system. His proposed fix is to push real budget and staffing authority down to principals. The generalizable governance point beyond education: if you want a role to be accountable for outcomes, its authority over the resources that drive those outcomes has to actually match that accountability, or the title is nominal.

Oki cites a concrete example of hidden administrative bloat: Washington state has 295 separate school districts, two of which have fewer than ten students and 62 of which have fewer than 200 -- smaller than a single Seattle elementary school -- yet each still carries its own superintendent salary of over $200,000 a year. The point isn't just that this is wasteful in the abstract; it's that bureaucratic redundancy can look individually reasonable at the local level (each small district has its own real reasons to exist) while being clearly wasteful in aggregate, which is why it survives despite being an obvious target for consolidation.

Oki's proposed Washington ballot initiative would force 80% of the state's $11 billion education budget to be spent directly in the classroom, up from roughly 70% today -- a 10-point shift worth over $1 billion a year, with no restriction on how it's spent (teacher pay, supplies, tutors) as long as it reaches the classroom. He benchmarks the aspiration against Costco, which runs on roughly 10% overhead, suggesting that if education administration matched that efficiency, more than $2 billion could flow to classrooms instead. The reusable move here is benchmarking a sector against an unrelated but genuinely efficient operator to size the opportunity, rather than arguing from ideology alone.
